title: The primal vow
hook: the vow that anyone who calls his name with faith will be born in his land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monk Dharmakara, who tied his own awakening to everyone else's. Your line was forty-eight vows. Did you keep the one you made for someone else? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

Of all Dharmakara's vows, which one is the door? Tradition says Pure Land teachers in China and Japan kept circling back to a single vow, and gave it a name of its own: the original vow, the root vow, in English often the primal vow. It doesn't describe jeweled trees or lotus ponds. Other vows do that. This one answers a plainer question, the one anybody would ask about a wonderful place far away. Who gets in? Today: the primal vow.
screen: `WHICH VOW IS THE DOOR?` → `WHO GETS IN?` → `THE PRIMAL VOW.`

segments.voice: First, the words, in paraphrase. When I become a Buddha, if beings anywhere in the ten directions entrust themselves to me sincerely and joyfully, wish to be born in my land, and call my name, even ten times, and are not born there, may I not attain perfect awakening. Same shape as yesterday. If not, not me. Second, what it asks, and what it doesn't. It doesn't ask for years on the cushion, a library of sutras, a monastery, money, or a spotless past. It asks for entrusting, for wishing, and for the name. The door is set low on purpose. A nurse finishing a night shift can walk through it. So can someone who never learned to read. Third, the hard clause. The vow ends with an exception: those who commit the gravest wrongs and slander the teaching. Pure Land teachers have wrestled with that line. Some read it as a warning meant to keep people from those harms, more than as a locked gate. Japanese schools that grew from this vow read it in their own ways, and the coming days will meet them. Fourth, why it's called primal. In Japanese the word is hongan, the original vow, the root one. The other vows describe the land; this one opens it. And remember how yesterday ended. The sutra says Dharmakara became a Buddha. So Pure Land teachers read the vow as already fulfilled, not a hope waiting to come true. In their telling, the door is not about to open. It's open.
screen: `THE WORDS OF THE VOW.` · `WHAT IT ASKS, AND WHAT IT DOESN'T.` · `THE HARD CLAUSE.` · `THE DOOR IS ALREADY OPEN.` · then, large: `THE PRIMAL VOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Pure Land Buddhists in Japan say Namu Amida Butsu. In China, Namo Amituofo. If this is your practice, say the name once, slowly and sincerely, and then rest. If it isn't, you can simply listen to the sound of it in your mind, the way you might listen to a neighbor's song through a wall. Either way, let the breath slow, and stay a while with the picture of a door offered, not earned. The bell holds the time.
The primal vow. Hongan in Japanese: Dharmakara's vow that those who entrust themselves to him, wish for his land, and call his name will be born there. Today's word.
Your line: the primal vow. Today, notice one door in your life you didn't earn: a welcome, a second chance, a kindness given first. Let it stay unearned. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists in East Asia treat this vow, hongan in Japanese, as the heart of the longer sutra; they call Amitabha's name, Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China, trusting that the vow has already been fulfilled.

fork.reveal: the vow sets the door low on purpose: entrusting, wishing and the name. no learning, wealth or spotless past required.

original.note: Japanese: hongan, the original or primal vow. the same characters are read benyuan in Chinese.

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise to be good.
what it means: Dharmakara's vow that those who entrust themselves and call his name will be born in his land.
what a scholar hears: hongan, the root vow, which Pure Land tradition counts as the eighteenth, with its hard exception clause.

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavati-vyuha (Sutra of Immeasurable Life), the vow on birth through the name (counted as the eighteenth)

notes: The vow is paraphrased from the Chinese version; 'even ten times' and the exception clause are in that text. Confirm paraphrase.
'Some read it as a warning more than a locked gate' alludes to Shandao's reading of the exclusion clause; left unattributed because day 1264 introduces Shandao. Confirm.
Counting it as 'the eighteenth' is attributed to Pure Land tradition; the Sanskrit versions number differently.
Hongan (本願) and the Chinese reading benyuan: confirm.
Practice invites the name only 'if this is your practice'; deeper teaching on calling the name, other power and entrusting is left to days 1263, 1265 and 1266.

Editor: unsourced history (teachers copied, preached on and argued over the vow) cut to 'tradition says'. The closing 'it's open' is now framed as how Pure Land teachers read the vow, not the narrator's own claim.
